 Best Sunscreen Brands in the World 2026
 La Roche-Posay tops our 2026 sunscreen ranking, ahead of NIVEA SUN and Neutrogena, as Bioré UV surges 24% and the FDA approves its first new filter in decades.
 How we rank: compiled from official product pages, company results and checked prices by the Global Brands Magazine editorial desk, with sponsored content kept separate and labelled. Last reviewed 11 November 2026. Editorial policy · Report an error 
 The best sunscreen brands in the world in 2026, judged on what their owners actually publish, are led by La Roche-Posay, the L’Oréal dermatology brand whose Anthelios range carries a filter built to reach ultra-long UVA light up to 400 nm. NIVEA SUN is second and Neutrogena third. Avène, Bioré UV, Banana Boat, Garnier Ambre Solaire, ANESSA, ISDIN and Beauty of Joseon make up the rest of the ten.
 It has been an unusual year. The US Food and Drug Administration approved its first new sunscreen active ingredient since the late 1990s, Kimberly-Clark bought Neutrogena’s owner, Kenvue, and Kao’s Bioré UV grew sales by 24%. We ranked the brands on published numbers and a disclosed weighting, say plainly where an owner publishes nothing, and keep the buying advice to what regulators and dermatologists’ societies say.

 Key Takeaways: 
 La Roche-Posay is our No 1 sunscreen brand for 2026. L’Oréal says its sun care “accelerated, driven by La Roche-Posay Anthelios” in the first nine months, when Dermatological Beauty sales rose 11.6% like-for-like to €6.09 billion (L’Oréal, 22 October 2026).
 NIVEA SUN was one of the two main growth drivers of the €5.53 billion NIVEA brand in 2025, but a late European sun season helped push NIVEA into decline in 2026 (Beiersdorf Annual Report 2025; half-year results 2026).
 Kao says Bioré UV sales grew 24% year on year as of June 2026, with a third of sales now made outside Japan in more than 30 countries and regions (Kao marketing briefing, 14 July 2026).
 The FDA added bemotrizinol to its permitted sunscreen ingredients on 9 June 2026, the first addition since the late 1990s.

 How we ranked the best sunscreen brands
 Sunscreen owners rarely report sales for a single brand, so we built a weighted score out of 100 from five criteria, using primary sources: annual and quarterly reports, SEC filings, results presentations, press releases and the brands’ own pages. Scale and disclosure (30 points) rewards brand or sun-care figures an owner actually publishes. Where nothing is published, a brand can earn at most half marks. Momentum (20) uses the latest reported trend, and an undisclosed trend scores a neutral 10. Ties are broken on the scale score. Global reach (20) reflects the countries an owner states for the brand. Protection science and range (15) covers filter technology, UVA performance, formats and specialist lines for children or sensitive skin. Heritage and trust (15) looks at age, influence on the category and any recalls on the public record.
 We did not test products in a laboratory. The scores are our editorial team’s judgement applied to the record, and no third-party league table or brand ranking was used. Where a company quotes market-research data in its own filing or release, we attribute it to that company. No brand paid to be included or saw the ranking before publication. This guide is part of our brand rankings series, alongside our guides to the top skincare brands in the world and the best cosmetic brands in the world .

 1. La Roche-Posay — the dermatology brand that pushed UVA protection to 400 nm
 On its brand page , L’Oréal describes La Roche-Posay as a dermatological brand recommended by more than 100,000 dermatologists, a company claim we cannot audit. L’Oréal does not publish the brand’s sales, but its nine-month release of 22 October 2026 says all three of the Dermatological Beauty Division’s “billionaire brands” grew at double digits, and names La Roche-Posay first. The division sold €6,087.4 million in the first nine months, up 11.6% like-for-like, and L’Oréal says “sun care accelerated, driven by La Roche-Posay Anthelios and the successful launch of CeraVe Sun”, with Anthelios UV Air among the launches. In 2025 it “remained the number one growth contributor” to the division, according to L’Oréal’s annual results .
 L’Oréal’s May 2022 release describes ten years of research behind Mexoryl 400, the filter in Anthelios UVMune 400, designed to absorb ultra-long UVA rays between 380 nm and 400 nm, which it says make up about 30% of UV. One caveat for American shoppers: US sunscreens may use only the active ingredients the FDA permits, so formulas sold there can differ from European ones.
 Pros: A filter that L’Oréal says reaches ultra-long UVA rays, double-digit growth in 2026, and a wide range from face fluids to body lotions.
 Cons: No brand-level sales disclosed, prices above supermarket brands, and US formulas can differ from European ones.
 Best for: Sensitive skin, daily face protection and anyone looking for long-UVA coverage where UVMune 400 is sold.
 2. NIVEA SUN — Europe’s supermarket staple, relaunched for 2025
 Beiersdorf’s Annual Report 2025 says the NIVEA brand, including Labello, had sales of €5,529 million in 2025, up 0.9% organically, and names Universal Creams and NIVEA Sun as its main growth drivers. The relaunched Protect & Moisture line, its largest NIVEA SUN range, reached more than 50 markets with what Beiersdorf calls CITRACELL-PROTECT technology, adding antioxidants to UVA and UVB filters. Beiersdorf says the launches helped it gain market share, particularly in Europe, and its products are sold in 180 countries.

 The weakness is 2026. Beiersdorf’s half-year results show NIVEA sales down 6.8% organically, partly because of “a later than expected sun season start in Europe”, and the third-quarter update of 27 October showed a further 4.9% decline, though sell-out to shoppers kept growing. Beiersdorf is spending its way back, and NIVEA SUN will become the official sun protection of the Tour de France in a five-year deal, announced on 21 October 2026, that starts in 2027.
 A free NIVEA SUN Protect & Moisture SPF 50+ dispenser in Berlin-Marzahn, June 2026. Photo: Singlespeedfahrer / Wikimedia Commons, CC0 (background extended)
 Pros: Sold almost everywhere, a refreshed core range and affordable family sizes.
 Cons: NIVEA’s 2026 sales are falling, and Beiersdorf does not publish a sun-only figure.
 Best for: Families who want a trusted, widely stocked SPF 30 or 50 at a sensible price.
 3. Neutrogena — America’s pharmacy favourite, now under Kimberly-Clark
 Kimberly-Clark’s third-quarter 10-Q confirms it completed the Kenvue acquisition on 2 November 2026, paying about $6.7 billion in cash and about 281.1 million shares. We covered the brands Kimberly-Clark just bought separately. Kenvue’s 2025 annual report shows total net sales of $15,124 million, of which the “Hair, Sun, and Other” category was 8%, roughly $1.2 billion. That includes hair care, so it is not a pure sun figure. Kenvue said a “softer sun season in the United States” weighed on 2025, but in its second-quarter 2026 results it named Neutrogena Ultra Sheer Sun among the launches that helped lift the segment’s net sales by 5.1%.
 A typical Ultra Sheer Dry-Touch SPF 70 label lists avobenzone, homosalate, octisalate and octocrylene as actives, with water resistance of up to 80 minutes. Trust costs it points: in July 2021 five Neutrogena and Aveeno aerosol sunscreen lines were recalled after internal testing found low levels of benzene in some samples.
 Pros: Huge US distribution, light “dry-touch” textures and a wide spread of SPF levels.
 Cons: The 2021 aerosol recall, no sun-only figures and a new owner.
 Best for: US shoppers who want a non-greasy, water-resistant sunscreen from any drugstore.
 4. Avène — a billion-euro pharmacy brand gaining share in sun care
 Pierre Fabre is privately controlled by a foundation, but its 2025 annual report gives Avène’s headline. Group revenue rose 4.6% to €3.2 billion, and Avène passed “the symbolic one-billion-euros in net sales”. The report says its sun care range won market share for the second year running, boosted by Ultra Fluid. Pierre Fabre’s annual report also says Avène “confirmed its position as global leader on the dermo-cosmetics market”, a company claim we cannot audit.
 Growth was led by China and the United States, where Avène sales rose 34.3% in 2025, driven notably by Cicalfate+ cream, according to the report.
 Pros: A billion-euro brand with sun care share gains in 2024 and 2025, and a strong record with sensitive-skin formulas.
 Cons: No sun-only figures, a mostly pharmacy-based distribution, and a US surge the report credits notably to Cicalfate+ cream.
 Best for: Pharmacy shoppers with reactive or easily irritated skin.
 5. Bioré UV — the fastest-growing brand here with published numbers
 At Kao’s marketing strategy briefing on 14 July 2026, the company said Bioré UV’s global sales were up 24% year on year as of June 2026, that 33% of sales now come from outside Japan, and that the line has reached more than 30 countries and regions, up from 27 in Kao’s full-year 2025 presentation . Kao, citing Circana data, says Bioré UV’s share of California’s facial UV care market passed 16% in May 2026.
 In Japan, Kao launched each generation of its Aqua Rich line through limited retailers first, from the 2021 Aqua Protect Lotion to the fifth-generation Airy Hold Cream, before going nationwide. It tested in Canada in 2024 and the US in 2025, and it entered South Korea in 2026, according to a Kao release issued ahead of a Seoul launch event on 19 March. Kao’s first-half results credit Bioré UV with growth in Japan, Asia and the Americas.
 Pros: Rapid disclosed growth and very light, watery textures.
 Cons: No absolute sales figure, and still small outside Asia and North America.
 Best for: People who hate the feel of sunscreen and want something closer to a water-light essence.
 6. Banana Boat — America’s beach bag brand
 Edgewell says it acquired Banana Boat with Playtex in 2007. In its 2025 Form 10-K , Edgewell says it believes Banana Boat and its sister brand Hawaiian Tropic together hold a leading share of US sun care, and that it is the leading sun care maker in Mexico, with a significant presence in Australia and Canada. The range runs from general protection to sport, kids, baby, tanning and after-sun.
 Edgewell’s Sun and Skin Care segment, which also includes men’s grooming and Wet Ones wipes, sold $743.1 million in the year to September 2025, but Sun Care fell 4.1% organically. In the quarter to June 2026, the third-quarter release reported mid-single-digit growth in North American sun care, offset by declines abroad, and the release lists “Sun Care reformulation” among its adjusted cost items. Full-year results are due on 12 November.
 Pros: A leading US position, strength in Mexico and a range for every beach need.
 Cons: Falling international sun sales, and no brand-level figures.
 Best for: Budget-minded families, sport and long days outdoors.
 7. Garnier Ambre Solaire — L’Oréal’s sun-care pioneer from 1935
 Ambre Solaire’s roots go back almost nine decades. L’Oréal’s official history records that Ambre Solaire was created in 1935, under the company’s founder, Eugène Schueller, “leading the way in sun protection oils”. It now sits within Garnier, which L’Oréal says on its Garnier page is present in 60 countries and lists Ambre Solaire among its iconic products.
 L’Oréal publishes nothing for Ambre Solaire itself, so it gets capped scale and neutral momentum scores, but full marks for heritage.
 Pros: Nine decades of history, L’Oréal research behind it and easy-to-find high-street prices.
 Cons: No published sales or growth figures, and a smaller footprint outside Europe.
 Best for: Shoppers in Britain and Europe who want a familiar name at a supermarket price.
 8. ANESSA — Shiseido’s summer-heat favourite, with a China problem
 ANESSA was born in 1992, according to an interview feature on Shiseido’s corporate site. The article describes an Auto-Repair technology that Shiseido says fixes gaps in the sunscreen film caused by movement. A 2024 Shiseido release listed the 12 Asian markets where ANESSA is sold, from Japan and China to Vietnam.
 In Shiseido’s second-quarter 2026 briefing of 5 August, management said ANESSA sales in China “continued to decline” as the company cut inventory, and that the brand needs to be repositioned there. In Japan, by contrast, it said ANESSA attracted new customers and strong repeat purchases.
 Pros: Sold in 12 Asian markets, with new customers and strong repeat purchases in Japan, and three decades of formulas for hot, humid summers.
 Cons: Falling China sales, little presence in Europe or the Americas, and no brand figures published.
 Best for: Sport, heat and humid summers, especially in East Asia.
 9. ISDIN — the Spanish photoprotection specialist Puig wants to own outright
 ISDIN began as a joint venture of Spain’s Puig and Esteve families, a partnership Puig’s chairman says spans five decades. On 14 September 2026 Puig agreed to buy Esteve’s 50% stake, and its third-quarter sales update of 21 October sets out the terms: €900 million in cash at closing, expected by the end of the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approvals, plus a fixed deferred payment of €300 million in the first quarter of 2029. ISDIN’s trading figures are reported, not published by the company: The Moodie Davitt Report reported that sun care makes up around half of ISDIN’s sales, that more than 70% of sales come from outside Spain, and that sales grew at a 17% compound annual rate from 2021 to 2025, with double-digit organic growth in the first half of 2026.
 Those are reported figures, so ISDIN’s scale score is capped. Its Fotoprotector ISDIN Fusion Water is a daily face fluid, and ISDIN’s website lists sun care for face, body, children and babies.
 Fotoprotector ISDIN Fusion Water SPF 50, a daily face sunscreen from the Spanish brand. Photo: Lubeel / Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA 4.0 (background extended)
 Pros: A sun specialist with fast reported growth, most of its sales reportedly made outside Spain, and light daily face fluids.
 Cons: No audited brand figures in the public domain, and Puig’s purchase is not expected to close until 2027.
 Best for: Daily face protection under make-up, bought from a pharmacy.
 10. Beauty of Joseon — the K-beauty sunscreen that went viral
 Beauty of Joseon was bought in 2019 by Goodai Global, whose portfolio also includes TIRTIR, SKIN1004 and Round Lab, according to a brand release of 9 June 2026 . Its hero product is Relief Sun, which the brand says grew on the back of organic consumer reviews. It has since added Relief Sun Aqua-Fresh and a Matte Sun Stick, both of which it says continue to show steady sales growth, and it names North America, Europe and South-East Asia as the regions where it has expanded since 2019.
 Goodai publishes no brand revenue, which caps scale. The brand earns its place on the growth it describes for its sun range, though it does not quantify it, and on how its light, skincare-like textures have changed what younger shoppers expect, a trend we explored in K-beauty’s global power play .
 Pros: A growing sun range, affordable prices and comfortable, dewy textures.
 Cons: No published sales figures, a short track record and formulas that vary by market because filter rules differ.
 Best for: Online shoppers who want a K-beauty texture for daily face wear.
 Also considered
 Coppertone , now owned by Beiersdorf, has one of the best-known names in American sun care, but Beiersdorf reported that its sales “remained significantly below the previous year” in 2025. Hawaiian Tropic , Eucerin Sun , CeraVe Sun and Kao’s Bondi Sands are reported inside wider businesses. Supergoop! , EltaMD , Ultra Violette , Sun Bum and Australian Gold are popular, but we found no primary financial disclosure to score them fairly.
 Sunscreen in 2026: a new filter, bad weather and big deals
 Three trends stand out. The first is regulation: on 9 June the FDA added bemotrizinol to the list of permitted sunscreen active ingredients, the first new one since the late 1990s. The agency said it protects against UVA and UVB rays and has long been used in Europe. Our explainer on America’s new sunscreen ingredient covers when it may reach shelves.
 The second is the weather. Beiersdorf blamed a late European sun season for part of NIVEA’s first-half decline, and Kenvue cited a softer US season in 2025. The third is consolidation, with Neutrogena now at Kimberly-Clark and ISDIN heading fully to Puig.
 How to choose a sunscreen: what dermatologists and regulators say
 The American Academy of Dermatology’s guide on how to select a sunscreen recommends a broad-spectrum product with SPF 30 or higher that is water resistant. In its sunscreen FAQs , the AAD says most adults need about one ounce, roughly a shot glass, and should reapply about every two hours, or after swimming or sweating. It says dermatologists recommend mineral sunscreens (zinc oxide or titanium dioxide) for sensitive skin. The British Association of Dermatologists’ sunscreen fact sheet also recommends SPF 30 or above, plus a UVA logo and, on UK products, a UVA rating of 4 or 5 stars.
 Labels differ by market. In the European Union, a Commission recommendation says UVA protection should be at least a third of the labelled SPF, sets “50+” as the top category, and rules out claims such as “sunblock” or “total protection”. In Australia, the Therapeutic Goods Administration treats primary sunscreens as therapeutic goods that must be in its register, requires SPF to be established under the AS/NZS 2604:2021 standard, and lists “50+” as the top claim, according to its regulatory guide . In June 2025 the TGA said it was investigating a consumer group’s report that some sunscreens missed their SPF claims. In the United States, the FDA’s consumer guidance says no sunscreen is waterproof, that water-resistant claims must state 40 or 80 minutes, and that sunscreen is not recommended for infants under six months, and that the best protection for them is to keep them out of the sun.
 For a beach or a sports pitch, a water-resistant lotion from Banana Boat, NIVEA SUN or Neutrogena does the job, while daily face wear suits the light fluids from La Roche-Posay, Bioré UV, ISDIN or Avène. Whatever you buy, the FDA advises using sunscreen together with other measures, such as shade and protective clothing, not instead of them.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What is the best sunscreen brand in the world?
 La Roche-Posay is the best sunscreen brand in the world in our 2026 ranking. L’Oréal reports double-digit growth for the brand in 2026, with sun care led by Anthelios, and its Mexoryl 400 filter is designed to cover ultra-long UVA rays up to 400 nm.
 What are the top 10 sunscreen brands?
 The top 10 sunscreen brands for 2026, on our weighted score of scale, momentum, reach, protection science and heritage, are La Roche-Posay, NIVEA SUN, Neutrogena, Avène, Bioré UV, Banana Boat, Garnier Ambre Solaire, ANESSA, ISDIN and Beauty of Joseon.
 Which sunscreen brand do dermatologists recommend?
 Neither the American Academy of Dermatology nor the British Association of Dermatologists names a brand in its sunscreen guidance. The AAD recommends a broad-spectrum, water-resistant sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher, about one ounce for most adults, reapplied about every two hours. The BAD recommends SPF 30 or above with a UVA logo and, in the UK, a UVA rating of 4 or 5 stars.
 Is SPF 50 better than SPF 30?
 Both the AAD and the BAD set SPF 30 as the minimum they recommend. The BAD notes that SPF and UVA protection are linked, so a higher-SPF sunscreen has more UVA protection, and the AAD stresses applying about one ounce and reapplying about every two hours.
 Why are European and American sunscreens different?
 In the US, sunscreens are regulated as over-the-counter drugs and may use only the active ingredients the FDA permits, so some brands sell different formulas in each market. Bemotrizinol, for example, was marketed in Europe for years before the FDA added it in June 2026, its first new sunscreen active ingredient since the late 1990s.
